{{< include _extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)


movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)

movies_clean <- movies |>
  separate_longer_delim(genre, delim = ", ")

movies_gap <- movies_clean |>
  mutate(gap = tomatoMeter - audienceScore)

movies_summary <- movies_clean |>
  filter(tomatoMeter > 0, audienceScore > 0) |>
  mutate(gap = tomatoMeter - audienceScore) |>
  summarize(mean_gap = mean(gap),
            n = n(),
            .by = genre) |>
  filter(n >= 100) |>
  arrange(mean_gap)

spiderman <- movies |>
  filter(title %in% c("Spider-Man", "Spider-Man 2", "Spider-Man 3",
                      "The Amazing Spider-Man", "The Amazing Spider-Man 2",
                      "Spider-Man: Homecoming", "Spider-Man: Far From Home",
                      "Spider-Man: No Way Home")) |>
  mutate(actor = case_when(
    str_starts(title, "The Amazing") ~ "Andrew Garfield",
    str_detect(title, ":") ~ "Tom Holland",
    .default = "Tobey Maguire")) |>
  arrange(releaseDateTheaters)
```

## Introduction

You will use AI to analyze roughly 30,000 films from Rotten Tomatoes, stored as a CSV. You will read the file, find the scores that are really missing values in disguise, measure how critics and audiences diverge by genre, and finish with the eight live-action Spider-Man films. Use AI however you like.

###

Rotten Tomatoes assigns every film two separate scores computed from completely independent sources — one from professional critics, one from verified ticket-buyers. The site was designed from the start to make both scores visible side by side, which is what makes it a useful dataset for comparing how differently these two groups respond to the same film.

###

The dataset covers roughly 30,000 films spanning 1902 to 2023 (essentially 1914 onward; the 1902 film is the only one before 1914). It was compiled from Rotten Tomatoes' public data and includes both the `tomatoMeter` (critic score) and `audienceScore` (audience score) for each film, along with genre, director, runtime, release date, and box office revenue.

## Exploring the data

The `movies.csv` file has 8 columns covering 29,783 films. Two matter most for this analysis: `tomatoMeter` (the critic score) and `audienceScore` (the audience score). A third column, `genre`, will need cleaning before it is useful.

## Critic vs. audience gap

The gap is `tomatoMeter - audienceScore`. A positive value means critics rated the movie higher than audiences; a negative value means audiences rated it higher.

### Exercise 1

Start a new working chunk that adds a `gap` column equal to `tomatoMeter - audienceScore` to `movies_clean` and stores the result as `movies_gap`. Below the assignment, show the title, both scores, and the gap for the first five rows. Render. In the R Terminal, run:

```r
show_file("analysis.qmd")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: gap-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Start a new working chunk that adds a gap column equal to tomatoMeter - audienceScore to movies_clean and stores the result as movies_gap. Below the assignment, show the title, both scores, and the gap for the first five rows. Render. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"analysis.qmd\"). CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: gap-1-answer
#| echo: true
movies_gap <- movies_clean |>
  mutate(gap = tomatoMeter - audienceScore)

movies_gap |>
  select(title, tomatoMeter, audienceScore, gap) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

###

The `gap` column measures the difference between professional critics and general audiences for each film. Films appear more than once in this tibble because `movies_clean` has one row per genre — a film with three genres will appear three times with the same `gap` value.

### Exercise 7

Add a horizontal bar chart of `movies_summary` showing average gap by genre, ordered from most audience-favored to most critic-favored, with a vertical line marking zero. Add a descriptive title and subtitle. Render, then take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}

learnr2::question(
  "Add a horizontal bar chart of movies_summary showing average gap by genre, ordered from most audience-favored to most critic-favored, with a vertical line marking zero. Add a descriptive title and subtitle. Render, then take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
```

###

```{r}
#| label: gap-7-answer
#| echo: true
movies_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_gap,
             y = fct_reorder(genre, mean_gap))) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Average Critic vs. Audience Score Gap by Genre",
       subtitle = "Positive = critics rate higher; Negative = audiences rate higher",
       x = "Mean Gap (Tomatometer − Audience Score)",
       y = "Genre")
```

###

Horror and Documentary rank at the top — critics consistently value them above audiences — while Action and Kids & family rank at the bottom. Comedy, the second most common genre, sits almost exactly at zero (−0.04): on the genre with the most films after Drama, critics and audiences agree.

## Spider-Man

Three actors have played Spider-Man on the big screen: Tobey Maguire, Andrew Garfield, and Tom Holland, across three different studios and eight films. Fans argue endlessly about who did it best — but "best" usually means one of two very different things: what critics thought, or what audiences thought. All eight films are in `movies`, so the gap you just measured by genre can settle whether critics and audiences agree on who the best Spider-Man is.

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">

###

```{r}

#| echo: true
spiderman <- movies |>
  filter(title %in% c("Spider-Man", "Spider-Man 2", "Spider-Man 3",
                      "The Amazing Spider-Man", "The Amazing Spider-Man 2",

  arrange(releaseDateTheaters)

spiderman |>
  select(title, releaseDateTheaters, actor, tomatoMeter, audienceScore)
```

###

Three films star Tobey Maguire (2002–2007, directed by Sam Raimi), two star Andrew Garfield (2012–2014, Marc Webb), and three star Tom Holland (2017–2021, Jon Watts, inside the Marvel Cinematic Universe). The animated *Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse* is also in `movies`, but it has no live-action lead, which is why it is left out.

###

```{r}
#| label: spider-man-2-answer

spiderman |>
  mutate(gap = tomatoMeter - audienceScore) |>
  select(title, actor, gap) |>
  arrange(desc(gap))
```

###

The original 2002 *Spider-Man* has the largest gap of the eight: critics scored it 23 points higher than audiences did. All three Maguire films sit on the critic side of zero, both Garfield films on the audience side, and the Holland films come closest to agreement, never more than 5 points apart.

### Exercise 3

Replace the table with a line chart of `tomatoMeter` and `audienceScore` across the eight films in release order, both lines on one plot with a legend telling them apart and a title that states the finding. Render, then take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: spider-man-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Replace the table with a line chart of tomatoMeter and audienceScore across the eight films in release order, both lines on one plot with a legend telling them apart and a title that states the finding. Render, then take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  allow_text = FALSE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: spider-man-3-answer
#| echo: true
spiderman |>
  mutate(title = fct_inorder(title)) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(tomatoMeter, audienceScore),
               names_to = "source", values_to = "score") |>
  mutate(source = if_else(source == "tomatoMeter", "Critics", "Audiences")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = title, y = score, color = source, group = source)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Tom Holland's Spider-Man films score highest with critics and audiences alike",
       subtitle = "Rotten Tomatoes scores for the eight live-action films, in release order",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Score",
       color = NULL,
       caption = "Source: Rotten Tomatoes") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

###

Averaged by actor, Holland's films score highest with both critics (91.7) and audiences (93.3), while Maguire's average 82.0 with critics but only 66.7 with audiences — critics liked his films far more than audiences did. Both lines dip together at each franchise's weakest entry, *Spider-Man 3* and *The Amazing Spider-Man 2*, so the two groups agree on which films are worst even when they disagree on the scores.

## Summary

In this tutorial you used AI to analyze a Rotten Tomatoes dataset stored as a CSV. You read the file and split the genre column, found the 628 zero scores that stand in for missing reviews, measured the critic-audience gap by genre, compared the three Spider-Man actors, and published the result.

###

Your `analysis.qmd` should look something like this:

````{verbatim}
---
title: "Movie Analysis"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
execute:
  echo: false
---

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
movies_clean <- movies |>
  separate_longer_delim(genre, delim = ", ")
```

```{r}
movies |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tomatoMeter)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Rotten Tomatoes Critic Scores",
       subtitle = "29,783 films",
       x = "Tomatometer Score",
       y = "Count")
```

```{r}
movies_gap <- movies_clean |>
  filter(tomatoMeter > 0, audienceScore > 0) |>
  mutate(gap = tomatoMeter - audienceScore)

movies_summary <- movies_gap |>
  summarize(mean_gap = mean(gap), n = n(), .by = genre) |>
  filter(n >= 100) |>
  arrange(mean_gap)

movies_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_gap, y = fct_reorder(genre, mean_gap))) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Average Critic vs. Audience Score Gap by Genre",
       subtitle = "Positive = critics rate higher; Negative = audiences rate higher",
       x = "Mean Gap (Tomatometer - Audience Score)", y = "Genre")
```

```{r}
spiderman <- movies |>
  filter(title %in% c("Spider-Man", "Spider-Man 2", "Spider-Man 3",
                      "The Amazing Spider-Man", "The Amazing Spider-Man 2",
                      "Spider-Man: Homecoming", "Spider-Man: Far From Home",
                      "Spider-Man: No Way Home")) |>
  mutate(actor = case_when(
    str_starts(title, "The Amazing") ~ "Andrew Garfield",
    str_detect(title, ":") ~ "Tom Holland",
    .default = "Tobey Maguire")) |>
  arrange(releaseDateTheaters)

spiderman |>
  mutate(title = fct_inorder(title)) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(tomatoMeter, audienceScore),
               names_to = "source", values_to = "score") |>
  mutate(source = if_else(source == "tomatoMeter", "Critics", "Audiences")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = title, y = score, color = source, group = source)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Tom Holland's Spider-Man films score highest with critics and audiences alike",
       subtitle = "Rotten Tomatoes scores for the eight live-action films, in release order",
       x = NULL, y = "Score", color = NULL,
       caption = "Source: Rotten Tomatoes") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```
````

###

Every chunk on the page draws on the same 29,783 films: the histogram uses all of them, the genre chart the 29,122 that have a real score on both measures, and the Spider-Man chart just eight.
